title: Yann LeCun Resurfaces Three-Year-Old Hearing Video to Blast Anthropic CEO: Stoking AI Fear Is an Attempt to Shackle Open Models

content_html:
A long-forgotten U.S. congressional hearing video from three years ago has dragged Turing Award winner Yann LeCun and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei back to opposite corners of the ring in the debate over AI openness. On November 22, LeCun reposted the July 25, 2023 Senate Judiciary Committee hearing video on X and directly called out Amodei. His accusation was sharp: since the GPT-2 era seven years ago, Amodei had been hyping the dangers of AI, with the real aim of getting open models banned by law and keeping control firmly in his own hands. LeCun argued that this would hinder the public’s free access to knowledge from different sources, and he slapped it with a harsh label—“a new form of medieval obscurantism.”

What angered LeCun was Amodei’s remarks at the hearing about “who can control models.” Amodei explained at the time that if a model is operated by its developer company, the company can monitor usage, revoke user permissions, and adjust which requests the model responds to; but once the weights are made public, others can download them and run them on their own devices, and the developer company can no longer take back access at all. In the same remarks, however, Amodei also acknowledged that open source can accelerate scientific progress and admitted that, as of the hearing, the risks of models already released to the public were relatively limited. What he truly worried about was whether, as frontier models’ capabilities continued to climb, companies had a way to contain hard-to-reverse risks after release before making stronger models public. This argument that “open weights are irreversible” is now being used by LeCun as evidence for his accusation.

What LeCun worries about is the other side of the coin: if only a few companies can run the most advanced models, who gets to decide which languages AI assistants can use and how they answer questions? In follow-up posts, he added his position—open foundation models allow different developers to build their own AI assistants on the same model to serve people of different languages, cultures, and interests. This was not the first time he made his stance clear: as early as 2025, when DeepSeek sparked widespread attention, he was still Meta’s chief AI scientist and publicly said that what he saw in it was that “open-source models are surpassing proprietary models.”

As for why he specifically brought up GPT-2, that goes back to 2019: in February of that year, OpenAI, citing concerns about misuse, released only a small version with 124 million parameters; it scaled up gradually in May and August, and only on November 5 did it release the full 1.5 billion-parameter version and its weights. Amodei and others were at OpenAI at the time, and in LeCun’s view, that history of “staged release” was the starting point of fear-mongering.

Interestingly, Amodei, who has been accused of “wanting to ban open-weight models,” had actually publicly denied it long ago. On July 27 of this year, he published a signed article on Anthropic’s website, explicitly stating that the company had never advocated banning open-weight models. He also wrote: for models without dangerous capabilities, open weights can benefit companies, developers, and researchers, with users simply bearing the compute cost of running the models themselves. On one side are the “safety camp,” who insist that models must be able to be recalled and controlled; on the other are the “openness camp,” who believe knowledge should not be monopolized by a few companies. This long-distance clash has no referee, but its outcome may well determine whether, in the coming years, AI ends up locked in a few people’s server rooms or scattered across everyone’s hard drives.
